sections.html:
Lakeville is the largest city in Dakota County, with 79,270 residents, about 20 miles south of both downtown Minneapolis and downtown St. Paul along Interstate 35. It grew 14.1 percent between April 2020 and mid-2025, and it covers about 36 square miles. New construction keeps arriving alongside resales, so a seller competes with fresh builds as well as other used houses.

The median owner-occupied home is valued at $452,500, and owners live in 87.8 percent of housing units. The city has 25,685 households averaging 2.89 people. Median household income is $139,041, owners with a mortgage pay a median $2,437 a month, and the commute averages 23.6 minutes. Median gross rent is $1,806, which is worth weighing if your house could be rented out instead of sold.

Interstate 35 is the main artery, and Cedar Avenue (Minnesota Highway 77) runs along the east side.

These rules matter if the house is rented now or you are thinking of renting it first. Since September 2023 Lakeville has required registration of long-term rentals, meaning stays of 32 days or longer. Registration is free and one-time unless contact information or ownership changes, and the city does not require inspections. An owner with several rentals files a form for each property.

Short-term rentals are allowed only with a Short-Term Rental Administrative Permit under Title 9, Chapter 10 of city code.

  • Listings must show the city permit number, maximum occupancy and maximum number of vehicles.
  • Overnight guests are capped at two adults per bedroom plus their dependent children.
  • Guest vehicles park in the garage or on the driveway, and noise must be reduced between 10:00 PM and 7:00 AM.
  • Owners pay local lodging tax under Title 3, Chapter 17 of city code.

A buyer who wants to run a rental after closing will ask whether the property is registered, so file the registration if you still hold the house as a rental.

• Full-service listing: makes sense when the house is current on maintenance and you can accept showings, appraisal timing and the buyer's financing conditions.
  • Direct cash sale: fits a house with deferred repairs, a probate or inherited property, or a rental where the lease complicates showings.
  • Selling it yourself: removes the agent fee but puts disclosures and negotiation on you.

Winters here are cold, so roof, furnace and insulation condition tend to draw buyer questions. Gather service records for those systems before you open the house to buyers. If the sale involves an inherited house, ask a title company whether the estate needs court paperwork before the deed can be signed.

sections.h2: Which school district is my house in?
sections.html:
Most Lakeville households are in Lakeville Area School District 194, which runs Lakeville North and Lakeville South high schools. Parts of northern and eastern Lakeville fall under District 196 (Rosemount-Apple Valley-Eagan) or Farmington District 192.

Because the boundaries date from the farming era, two neighbors can be in different districts. Minnesota's open enrollment law also lets families choose a school outside their home district. Name the exact district for the address in your listing so buyers do not have to guess.

Lakeville bills residential water quarterly and calculates sewer charges from winter-quarter water use. The city's Form Center has an online stop-service form for sellers and a start-service form for buyers. You can pay bills through InvoiceCloud, by mail, or at City Hall at 20195 Holyoke Avenue. Call the Utility Division at 952-985-2700 with questions about the meter, and ask for a final read that matches your closing date.

sections.h2: Recording the deed and paying property tax
sections.html:
Dakota County Property Taxation and Records records Lakeville deeds at its Hastings office. State deed tax is 0.0033 of the net price. The county auditor must confirm there are no delinquent taxes before the deed can be recorded (Minnesota Statutes 272.12), and Minnesota Statutes 513.55 requires you to give the buyer a written disclosure of material facts before signing a purchase agreement.

sections.h2: Selling a house that is rented
sections.html: A tenant in place changes the timeline. Showings need notice, and a lease may run past the day a retail buyer wants to move in. Read the lease for its end date and any renewal option, then decide whether to wait it out, offer the tenant a move-out agreement, or sell to a buyer who will keep the renter. Hand over the lease, the rent history and the city registration so the buyer sees a clean file. Security deposits transfer or are returned at closing, so settle that with the title company in writing.

sections.h2: Selling a newer house against new construction
sections.html: Because builders keep adding homes, buyers can compare your house with a brand-new one down the road. Lean on what a resale offers: a finished yard, mature landscaping and a known street. Note any updates to the kitchen, roof or furnace with dates. If the house needs work that would cost more than a retail buyer will credit, an as-is cash offer lets you skip the comparison and the repair bill.

sections.h2: Prepare the property before buyers arrive
sections.html: Walk the lot as a buyer would. Fix loose railings, clear the gutters, test smoke detectors and make sure the furnace and water heater run. List any known leaks or past water in the basement, because the disclosure covers what you know. Keep the list short, specific and dated, and attach receipts where you have them. It is better for a buyer to read about an old repair from you than to find it during an inspection.

sections.h2: What to have ready before closing
sections.html: Keep your latest tax statement, the parcel number, any rental registration and the keys together. Schedule the water meter read, ask the county for a payoff if taxes are owed, and confirm with the title company who files the deed. If tenants live in the house, give the buyer the lease and the registration details. A cash buyer can often work around a lease, which a retail buyer usually cannot. At closing you sign the deed, hand over keys and garage openers, and receive your proceeds after the title company pays off any mortgage and taxes owed.

faqs.a: Lakeville is the largest city in Dakota County, at 79,270 people. Its size means a large pool of potential buyers and a lot of new construction competing with resales.

faqs.q: Do I need to register my Lakeville rental before selling it?
faqs.a: Lakeville requires registration of residential rentals of 32 days or longer, with no fee and no inspection. Register each property once, and update the city if ownership or contact information changes.

faqs.q: Can a buyer run a short-term rental in a Lakeville house?
faqs.a: Only with a Short-Term Rental Administrative Permit from the city, and the owner must follow the Title 9, Chapter 10 performance standards. Those include listing the permit number and limiting guests to two adults per bedroom.

faqs.q: How much deed tax will I see on a Lakeville sale?
faqs.a: State deed tax is 0.0033 of the net price above $3,000. Your title company will show the exact figure on the closing statement.

faqs.q: Who do I contact to stop Lakeville utilities when I sell?
faqs.a: Use the Finance forms on the city's Form Center to stop service, or contact the Utility Division at 952-985-2700. Bills are quarterly, so ask for a final read that matches your closing date.
